Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 43
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: In a relationship
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 80

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Emotional Numbing: I numb my feelings, Avoid Positive Events: Situations that might make me feel happy or hopeful, Delay Sleep: stay up until very late
  Threat: Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Emotions: I will never be able to feel normal emotions again, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Physical Vulnerability: My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

Vignette:
Mara, a 43-year-old chef, had always trusted her body. It had carried her through fifteen-hour shifts in sweltering kitchens, through the precise knife work and the relentless pace of service. That trust shattered two years ago, when a sudden, crushing pain in her chest turned out not to be exhaustion but a pulmonary embolism that nearly killed her. She remembers the emergency room with a clarity that feels less like memory and more like being pulled back into that moment: the fluorescent lights, the cold plastic of the oxygen mask, the frantic voices of the doctors, and the terrifying sensation of her own lungs refusing to work. When the memory comes now, it is not a recollection but a full sensory reliving—she can taste the metallic tang of blood in her mouth, feel the sweat on her palms, hear the monitor’s alarm as if it is happening in the next room. And yet, at the same time, the whole experience feels so extreme, so surreal, that she sometimes finds herself thinking it could not possibly have happened to her. It is a story that belongs to someone else, except that her body keeps telling her otherwise.

In the months following her discharge, Mara tried to return to her life. She went back to the restaurant, but the kitchen had become a minefield. The heat of the stovetop made her heart race before her mind had even registered why. The smell of antiseptic from the cleaning supplies would trigger a full flashback—suddenly she was back on the gurney, unable to breathe, her body reacting to danger before she had time to think. She learned to dread the moments when a customer would laugh loudly or when a sous-chef would clap her on the back in congratulations; those moments of happiness or hope felt dangerous, as if feeling good might somehow invite the disaster to return. She began avoiding positive events altogether, turning down invitations to dinner with friends, refusing to celebrate a successful service. What frightened her most was the growing conviction that she would never feel normal emotions again. The grief she carried was overwhelming—not just for her brush with death, but for the person she used to be, the one who could move through the world without this constant, watchful dread.

Her sleep became a battleground. She stayed up until very late, sometimes past two or three in the morning, because the moment she closed her eyes, the reliving would start. She would feel the pressure in her chest, hear the beeping of the monitors, and wake gasping. So she delayed sleep, scrolling through her phone or staring at the television, knowing she was exhausted but unable to surrender to the dark. Her partner, a gentle man named David, would find her on the couch at dawn, her body rigid, her eyes fixed on nothing. He tried to hold her, but Mara had learned to numb her feelings so thoroughly that she could not even access the comfort of his arms. She had come to believe that her body was her enemy—that it kept reacting as if she were still in danger even when she was safe, that it had been permanently damaged by what happened. Every skipped heartbeat, every twinge of muscle, every moment of breathlessness felt like proof that her body was broken beyond repair.

The consequences accumulated quietly. At work, she began delegating the tasks that required sustained physical effort, afraid that a heavy pot or a sudden sprint to the walk-in cooler might trigger another collapse. Her sous-chef noticed, and then the owner noticed, and Mara was moved from the line to a more administrative role—a demotion in everything but title. She felt the loss acutely, but she could not explain why she could no longer handle the heat of the kitchen. She could not relax, not even in her own home, because she was certain that danger was always waiting, that her body would betray her again the moment she let her guard down.

What finally brought her to seek help was not the flashbacks or the sleeplessness, though those had worn her thin. It was a single moment, three weeks ago, when David asked her to go for a walk on a sunny afternoon. She wanted to say yes. She wanted to feel the warmth on her skin. But the thought of feeling happy—of letting herself hope for a good day—sent a spike of terror through her chest, and she said no. She watched his face fall, and she realized she had become a ghost in her own life. She is terrified that she will never get back the person she was, that the damage is permanent. But she has come to this office anyway, because she is even more afraid of losing David, of losing her career, of spending the rest of her life numbed and watchful in a body she no longer trusts.
